# Miami, round two

The first round is in this folder and is committed: 85 tiles in four zooms, the base layers, the style sheet, every original painting, the report. Read `BRIEF.md`, `REPORT.md`, `STATE.md`, `style/STYLE.md` and `tools/mapart/README.md`, and look at the tiles before anything else.

## What round one got right, and must keep

- It is true to the data. Coasts, roads and buildings sit where the layers put them.
- No seam shows. Measured independently across all 140 tile joins, the jump across a join is the jump beside it (worst 1.29 times).
- The zooms agree. Each zoom shrunk onto the one above differs by under 2 of 255 in broad colour.
- The nearest zoom has real richness: roofless blocks with rooms, palms and scrub through them, flooded streets, pale shallows.
- Everything is reproducible from the saved originals.

## Why there is a round two

The bar was "a map someone would frame". Round one is an accurate, handsome, tinted plan. It is not yet a drawn map, and the project's owner has asked that work short of the bar be done again, with no limit on time or cost: "aim for the stars". These are the reasons, as seen by someone looking at the pictures, not at the numbers.

1. **The far zooms are not drawn for their scale.** Zoom 0 shows every building and every street of the city at eight metres a pixel. It reads as a street plan seen from far away: a grey-and-tan mesh. An explorer drawing the whole bay would not draw eleven thousand buildings. They would draw the districts as masses with their own character, a handful of landmarks as small pictures (a cluster of ruined towers, the port's sheds and cranes, the broken bridges), bold coasts, and the water. Round one's own report says this: "the exact city fabric is denser at zoom 0 than a freely generalized explorer's atlas would be". At the far zooms, be true to the coast, the islands, the causeways and the main roads, and generalise the rest. The game draws coloured cells for players' bases and markers over the map, so the far zooms need room to breathe.
2. **The shore is a ruled line.** Every coast and island edge is a razor-straight vector edge with one dark line of one weight. It looks like survey output laid under a painting. A drawn coast has a line that thickens and thins, wavers a little, breaks at a beach and doubles at a quay, with shallows that follow it. "Within a couple of pixels" leaves room for a hand.
3. **The story is faint.** This is Miami long after people. At the far zooms the causeways look intact, the streets look dry and the city looks inhabited. The flooded streets, the broken spans, the wrecks and the mangrove taking the shore back should be what the eye finds first at every zoom, drawn for that zoom.
4. **There is no paper.** The style sheet shows ivory rag paper under ink and wash. The tiles are colour from edge to edge. Let the paper show through the washes, most of all on land, and let ink hatching carry relief and density.
5. **The city is one texture.** Downtown towers, low houses, port sheds, parks gone to jungle and beach hotels are all drawn with the same mark. Give each district its own.

## What to do

Paint it again where it falls short, with a free hand as before. Keep what is already at the bar: much of zoom 3 may only need its coasts inked and its districts told apart. Zoom 0 and zoom 1 most likely need a new approach, and zoom 2 some of each. Decide for yourself, by looking.

Before you call it finished, put the whole-map zoom beside the best illustrated maps you know of from any game or atlas and ask which one a stranger would hang on a wall. Keep going until it is this one. Say plainly in the report where it still falls short.

What must hold is unchanged: true to the data at each zoom for what that zoom draws, no seams, zooms that agree in broad colour, tiles of 1,024 pixels named as before, no lettering, border, compass or grid.

## Two practical things

- **The engine counts x the other way.** The repository now has a map file format (`planning/reference/maps.md`, `tools/map.ts`). In it, pictures are north up as the map screen shows them, places are metres from the map's south-east corner, and x grows to the west. Your layers and vectors count easting to the east from the centre. Do not build a map file yet (the format is about to gain a second version), but add to `base/VALUES.md` the exact rule from your coordinates to the engine's, checked against that document, so whoever builds the world cannot get it mirrored.
- **What is kept in the repository** is the artwork and what made it. `assets/source/maps/miami/.gitignore` now leaves out the downloads, the reference renders, the check pictures and the warped copies, since your tools make them again. Keep anything a reader needs to judge the work (measurements, the production log) in `REPORT.md` or beside it, not under `checks/`. Replace round one's tiles and originals in place; history keeps the old ones. Do not run git commands that write: the work is committed for you when the run ends.

Network access is on. The virtual environment under `tools/mapart/.venv` is still there.

# A painted map of Miami

You are making the in-game world map for a survival game: the picture a player opens to see where they are. This is the first painted map the project has, and it is the example every later map will be held to. You have a free hand in how you do it. This brief says what it is for, what excellent looks like, what must hold, and what we learned from a first test. It is guidance, not a procedure.

## What it is for

The game is a survival game in the manner of ARK: Survival Evolved, with its own original art. Its maps will be ruined, overgrown cities built from public geographic data. The first is Miami.

The map screen shows a painted picture of the world with a coordinate grid over it (latitude and longitude from 0 to 100, as ARK has), player markers, and coloured cells where bases stand. The game draws the grid, the markers and the cells itself, over your picture. So the picture has to be true to the world: a coast on the map is a coast in the game.

The map has four zooms, baked in advance. Zoom 0 is the whole map in one tile. Each zoom doubles: 2 by 2 tiles, 4 by 4, and 8 by 8 at zoom 3. Every tile is a square picture, 1,024 pixels a side. Each zoom is its own picture drawn for its scale, not a shrunk copy of the one below.

## The example

A square of Miami about 8 km on a side, north up: downtown, the port, Biscayne Bay and its causeways, South Beach. The engine's ground grid is 2 m cells in chunks of 64 m, and the largest map it takes today is 127 chunks, 8,128 m, so make the square exactly that and say where its corners are.

It is Miami long after people: flooded streets, mangrove taking the shore back, towers standing as ruins, causeways broken, the beach wide and wild. Recognisably Miami in its coastline, street pattern and districts.

Painted in the manner of ARK's in-game maps, by description: aged parchment, confident ink linework, watercolour washes, shorelines with a darker ink edge and pale shallows, relief and built-up areas shown with hatching and small drawn symbols. A map an explorer drew. Describe the style to the image tool in words and build our own style sheet; do not give it other games' map pictures.

## The bar

A map someone would frame. Better than our test map, which is the example to beat: `planning/artist-test/map/map_1024.png` and its two double-zoom quarters, with the brief that made them in `planning/artist-test/briefs/map.md` and the report in `planning/artist-test/map/REPORT.md`.

- One hand across all four zooms: the same palette, line weight and symbols, so zooming feels like leaning closer to one drawing.
- Each zoom drawn for its scale. The far zoom broad and bold: the bay, the islands, the districts as shapes. The near zoom rich: individual ruined blocks, causeway spans, mangrove edges, sandbars, wrecks, the grid of streets.
- Detail that rewards looking, and no mush: nothing that reads as filler or noise.
- No lettering, no compass rose, no border and no grid lines in the tiles. The game draws its own grid and labels.

## What must hold

- **True to the data.** Every coast, island, road and built block is where the data puts it, to within a couple of pixels at each zoom.
- **No seams.** Tile joins to tile with nothing to see, across and down, at every zoom.
- **Zooms agree.** A zoom shrunk to the scale of the one above shows the same world in the same colours.

Measure these your own way and report the numbers. They will also be measured independently.

## The data

Public-domain and CC0 sources already identified for Miami:

- The 2021 Miami-Dade LiDAR hosted by NOAA (CC0), with points classified as ground, buildings, vegetation, water and bridges, and the bare-earth elevation raster made from it.
- USGS 3DEP elevation (public domain).
- Census TIGER roads (CC0 in the federal catalogue).
- FEMA USA Structures building outlines.
- USGS NLCD land cover.

Use only sources whose licence lets the result be redistributed freely, and record each one.

Make base layers on the map's own grid (4,065 samples a side at 2 m, or finer if it helps the painting): height, water, land cover, roads, building blocks. These same layers will later become the playable world through the engine's map file, so the painting and the world agree by construction. Keep them as plain files (16-bit PNG for height, 8-bit PNG for classes) with a note saying what each value means.

## What the first test taught

- Work out a style sheet and palette before the big pictures: how sea, shallows, beach, mangrove, swamp, ruin blocks, causeways, roads and height are each drawn. Then every picture is made against it and biomes stay consistent.
- The image tool returns pictures of about 1,254 pixels a side whatever is asked, which suits one tile per picture.
- The image tool alone does not hold a shoreline in place. In the test the painting was warped and composited against the water mask, which made it exact. That worked; better ideas are welcome.
- Give each zoom a reference rendered at that zoom's own resolution. In the test the double-zoom tiles followed an enlarged mask and their shores came out stepped.
- Painting a tile with its neighbours' edges and the zoom above as context kept the hand consistent and the seam invisible.
- Every accepted picture is a reference for the next.

## Where things go

Everything lives in the repository so another team can pick it up and see how it was made.

- `assets/source/maps/miami/`: this brief, `SOURCES.md` (each dataset: address, licence, date, checksum, what was taken), the base layers, the reference renders, the style sheet, every accepted picture, the finished tiles as `tiles/z<zoom>/<column>_<row>.png` with column 0 at the west and row 0 at the north, and `REPORT.md`.
- `assets/source/maps/miami/raw/`: downloads. Keep this folder out of git with a `.gitignore`, since the datasets are large and `SOURCES.md` says how to fetch them again.
- `tools/mapart/`: whatever tools you write, with a short `README.md` saying what each does and how to run it. Python is fine here. The engine and its build have no outside dependencies and that will not change, so keep any packages your tools need in a virtual environment inside `tools/mapart/` that git ignores, and list them with versions. No geodata libraries are installed on this machine; writing a small reader of your own for a format is welcome where practical.
- Touch nothing else in the repository. Do not run git commands that write: your work is committed for you when a run ends.

## How to work

- Work in stages and keep your state on disk: a short `STATE.md` saying what is done, what is accepted and what is next, so that a later run can carry on from it.
- Show something whole early. A good order is the style sheet, zoom 0, zoom 1, then one district carried all the way down to zoom 3, then the rest.
- Look at your pictures. Iterate until you would ship them.
- Several tiles can be worked at once if you can keep the hand consistent.
- Disk is plentiful (about 300 GB free). Network access is on for downloading the data.

## Report

Write `assets/source/maps/miami/REPORT.md` as you go: what you made and how, the sources, your measurements, what you are proud of, what falls short of the bar and why, and how long each stage took. End each run by saying plainly where things stand.
# Miami — the drowned atlas

**Complete and accepted for this delivery.** Produced 2026-11-14, 17:28–19:38 UTC (about 2 h 10 min wall time). All 85 independently painted tiles, shared geographic layers, references, originals, prompts, measurements and reproduction tools are present.

## Delivery and geography

This is an original painted atlas of an **8,128 × 8,128 m** square: downtown and Brickell, the port, Biscayne Bay, the Venetian and other island chains, South Beach, Fisher Island, and northern Virginia Key. The projection is a local WGS84 Transverse Mercator centred at 25.78° N, 80.166° W, scale 1. Bounds are −4,064 to +4,064 m on both axes. North is up; grid/true-north convergence is below 0.018° at the edges.

| Corner | Longitude | Latitude |
|---|---:|---:|
| Northwest | −80.2065295168 | 25.8166780455 |
| Northeast | −80.1254704832 | 25.8166780455 |
| Southeast | −80.1254954055 | 25.7433104873 |
| Southwest | −80.2065045945 | 25.7433104873 |

| Zoom | Canvas | Tiles | Metres per pixel |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1,024² | 1 | 7.9375 |
| 1 | 2,048² | 4 | 3.96875 |
| 2 | 4,096² | 16 | 1.984375 |
| 3 | 8,192² | 64 | 0.9921875 |

Every game tile is 1,024 × 1,024 RGB PNG, named `tiles/z<zoom>/<column>_<row>.png`, west to east and north to south. Tiles contain no lettering, border, compass or coordinate grid. `checks/viewer.html` provides an offline review viewer with optional separate overlays. `paintings/z*/final-master.png` stores the uncut canvases; `checks/overview_z*.png` provides small previews.

The engine foundation consists of 4,065 inclusive samples at 2 m spacing: exactly 4,064 cells, or 127 chunks of 64 m. Height is 16-bit PNG; classifications are 8-bit PNG. Canonical water, road, building and authored-canopy masks are additionally retained at 8,192² so narrow features survive world placement. [Layer encodings](base/VALUES.md) explain units, values, vertex versus image-pixel registration, and the normalized 0–100 overlay transform. `map.json` is the machine-readable geographic contract.

## Sources and fictional changes

[SOURCES.md](SOURCES.md) records addresses, licences, attribution and what was taken. [downloads.json](downloads.json) records exact requests, dates, byte counts and SHA-256 checksums. Downloads are ignored under `raw/`.

- NOAA's 2021 Miami-Dade bare-earth DEM: 369 intersecting tiles, CC0. Converted from NAVD88 US survey feet to metres. Valid coverage includes **99.9714% of source land samples**; 2,203 land samples are missing. Surveyed heights range from −5.53 to 17.18 m.
- Census TIGER/Line 2025: 38 clipped hydrography polygons and 1,184 road features, public domain/CC0. These define the shore and road centrelines.
- FEMA/ORNL USA Structures: 11,919 clipped building footprints. The federal catalogue describes a government work, but the delivery item declares CC BY 4.0. Attribution is retained conservatively; include SOURCES.md when redistributing.
- USGS NLCD 2021: public-domain land-cover classes at their actual approximately 30 m source resolution.

Road widths are authored corridors around the source centrelines. Future mangrove/reclamation, low street flooding, four broken causeway spans and four submerged wrecks are explicit world layers. Added tree crowns were frozen from the complete registered finest-scale paintings, then reused by every zoom: 6,878,251 fine pixels, with a 4,065-sample companion for the engine. These changes describe an invented future, not present-day surveys.

## How the painting was made

The original [style sheet](style/style-sheet.png) and [written style specification](style/STYLE.md) came first: ivory rag paper, warm quill ink, limestone ruins, olive foliage, mineral-teal water and pale jade shallows. No other game's map image or commercial basemap was supplied to image generation. The earlier project test was inspected as a quality comparison.

Each zoom received a newly rasterized geographic reference at its own resolution. All **85 tiles have a separately generated original painting**; none of the final zooms is a resized lower-level painting. The image tool returned approximately 1,254 px squares. Finer paintings include 64 px overlap around a 1,024 px tile, and were made against the native geometry, a crop of the accepted parent painting, and the shared style sheet. All original outputs, used prompts and context crops are preserved.

Image generation alone did not preserve geography. Finishing registers the pigment to geographic corners using position-constrained SIFT/RANSAC similarity fits, with a multistart main-water-silhouette fit in sparse scenes and a small smooth local shoreline correction. Original paint supplies washes, quill texture, foliage and ruin interiors. Exact native vector masks control every visible coast, road corridor and building silhouette. A continuous shallow wash repairs exposed water without dragging masonry or tree fragments into the bay. Interior ruin partitions are illustrative, not surveyed floorplans.

Overlapping paint is blended with smooth 128 px transitions on one continuous canvas per zoom. Geometry and colour finishing then run across the entire canvas before it is cut into tiles. Broad material-local pigment matching keeps parent colours stable while retaining separately painted close detail. The finest authored canopy is shared by all zooms and saved with world data.

The final format audit passed: **85 RGB 1,024² tiles, 85 original paintings, all required prompts, grayscale base layers with correct sizes and bit depths**, and SHA-256 inventory. Whole-map views, the complete 64-tile closest-scale sheet, native downtown/island/port/beach/mangrove tiles, and joined-corner crops were inspected. No visible tile joins or accidental lettering were found. See [zoom comparison](checks/zoom_comparison.jpg), [joined corners](checks/native_seams.jpg), and [all close-scale tiles](checks/final_z3.jpg).

The additional engine-grid check exposed a half-open polygon endpoint convention and surface-road/tunnel overlap. Endpoint classes and tunnel precedence were corrected. The **canonical fine masks have zero differing pixels and zero boundary error** against the finest geographic references. The 2 m companions still quantize narrow source features:

| 2 m companion versus finest vectors | IoU | 95th-percentile boundary distance | Maximum boundary distance |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| water | 0.998298 | 1 px | 4.000 px |
| roads | 0.907230 | 1 px | 23.195 px |
| buildings | 0.921490 | 1 px | 117.209 px |

The large maxima include very narrow/disappearing pieces and boundaries truncated by the map frame; they do not indicate a translation of the whole layer. **Do not use only the 2 m companions to reconstruct all fine outlines. Use `*_fine.png` or the supplied vectors for world feature placement.** Their finer resolution is necessary to preserve all source detail. The base height grid remains exactly 4,065².

Machine-readable results: [paint measurements](checks/measurements.json), [base-grid comparison](checks/base_grid_agreement.json), [delivery audit](checks/delivery_audit.json), and [endpoint corrections](checks/canonical_layers.json).

The geographic test classifies the final RGB pigments into water, roads and buildings, then compares those visible regions to native vector-derived masks. Water includes authored flooded streets; surface occlusion by bridges/buildings and authored bridge gaps is accounted for. These tests measure agreement with the supplied data, not the absolute surveying accuracy of that data. The distinct material palettes make the result directly inspectable; zero boundary error is a consequence of the constrained finish, not evidence that the image model traced perfectly.

Seam tests reconstruct every tile into its canvas and measure colour jumps at joins against nearby non-join boundaries. Parent comparisons use a 2× box reduction, with both raw RGB differences and an 8 px blurred comparison to separate native ink detail from broad colour agreement. Visual inspection remains necessary: correct masks alone did not catch the foliage and ghost-shoreline defects rejected during development.

## Artistic assessment and limits

The strongest result is the combination of Miami's distinctive island/port geometry with luminous water and fine, footprint-specific masonry. The pale street network remains legible beneath a game overlay; the closer drawings add room walls, courtyards, vegetation, flooded reaches and small wreck ribs without moving the world. Water-dominated tiles preserve open space.

The exact city fabric is denser at zoom 0 than a freely generalized explorer's atlas would be. That is the principal artistic compromise made to preserve every supplied building and road. Ruin interiors are symbolic, and some large structures still read as shaded masonry masses rather than fully exposed floorplans. Mangrove crowns are authored marks without surveyed heights. This is a map-art and shared-layer delivery, not a finished 3D terrain or building reconstruction.

TIGER is cartographic rather than a cadastral shoreline survey, FEMA omits some small structures, and source dates differ. Neither road widths nor individual tree crowns are measured. No bathymetry was acquired: missing DEM values use an explicit −1 m engine convention with a separate validity mask. Shallow-water colour is artistic and does not encode measured depth. NOAA point-cloud classifications and USGS 3DEP were not used because the selected DEM, footprints and land cover supplied the required layers.

# The drowned atlas — original Miami map style

An explorer's carefully observed field atlas, on pale warm rag paper. Quiet, luminous washes and crisp economical pen strokes; no sepia fog, heavy vignette or ornamental frame. Geometry is planar, north up. Tiny ruin symbols stay inside their real footprints.

## Pigment anchors

| Material | RGB hex | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Paper / high sand | #E5D8B5 | Warm ivory rag; subtle fine tooth |
| Land wash | #C9C49D | Pale straw-sage; breathing room between ink marks |
| Open sea | #568580 | Muted mineral teal, broad calm watercolor blooms |
| Deep channels | #406E70 | Blue slate teal; restrained darker wash |
| Shallows | #A3C6B5 | Luminous pale jade inside the water edge |
| Beach | #E7D4A2 | Wide soft cream-gold ribbon; fine dune hatching |
| Mangrove | #7B8660 | Olive and sage foliage masses; tiny root hooks |
| Swamp | #9BA385 | Pale olive reeds over watery jade |
| Ruin masonry | #B1A48A | Warm limestone roofs, broken outlines, crisp hatch |
| Ink | #514B38 | Warm charcoal, confident thin pen; never pure black |
| Roads | #DCD0AA | Exposed paper ribbons with fine broken ink shoulders |
| Rust accent | #96704B | Sparse wreck/rubble marks; never a broad district fill |

## Symbols and scale

Sea has no invented islands or decorative compass. Shallows are derived from the true coast (a visual depth convention, not surveyed bathymetry). Beaches follow mapped low bare ground. Mangroves occupy actual vegetation/derived succession polygons. Swamp is sparse reed ticks, never dense fuzz. Building marks are clipped to true footprints: roofless limestone shells, courtyard voids, directional wall hatching. Roads are exact centerline corridors; causeways retain the real alignment. Any fictional break must also be recorded in a world-change layer.

Zoom 0: districts, bay and islands read immediately; main avenues and large ruin clusters. Zoom 1: blocks, causeways, canals and beach ribbons. Zoom 2: individual structures and grove edges. Zoom 3: roofless walls, small alleys, bridge spans, roots, sand ripples and submerged debris. Use the same pigment family and apparent ink weight at every zoom, with richer symbols at closer scales.

Never put lettering, a grid, compass, neatline, legend or page edge into a game tile. The separate style sheet may have sample captions. No mountainous relief: Miami is low and flat. No gratuitous noise or repeated decorative stamps.
# Miami map-art tools

Offline source/art tools only. They add no dependency to the engine or its build.

From the repository root, create the isolated environment:

```sh
python3 -m venv tools/mapart/.venv
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/pip install -r tools/mapart/requirements.txt
```

The frozen bounds, projection and sample conventions are in `assets/source/maps/miami/map.json`. Python 3.9 was used; exact package versions are pinned. Raw data and the virtual environment are ignored by git.

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| fetch.py | Download intersecting NOAA DEM tiles, county TIGER ZIPs, NLCD coverage and paginated FEMA footprints. Write exact request URLs and SHA-256 checksums to downloads.json. Reuses existing downloads. |
| prepare.py | Clip/reproject vectors, reproject bare-earth height, rasterize 4,065 vertex samples, preserve NLCD codes, author explicit succession and low-street flooding. Checks FEMA pages against the complete object-ID inventory. |
| future.py | Freeze four missing bridge spans and four submerged wrecks as shared world geometry; mark tunnels as subterranean. Run after prepare.py. |
| reference.py [zooms...] | Render geographic references afresh from the vector data at each native zoom, with water/road/building masks. Default: all four zooms. |
| contexts.py Z | Build each tile's 64 px neighboring overlap, parent-paint context, exact prompt and queue.json for the built-in image tool. |
| finish.py Z | Similarity registration, local shoreline registration, class-constrained pigment and architectural detail, overlapping assembly, parent-color matching, exact cutting into 1,024 px PNGs. Requires every original painting for that zoom. |
| finish.py Z --partial | Pilot only: export already-painted tiles while keeping explicitly provisional parent proxies under checks/partial_zZ.png. Never use partial images as a completed delivery. |
| alignment.py | Position-constrained SIFT/RANSAC registration of original ink against geographic corners, with multistart main-water-silhouette similarity fitting for sparse scenes. Used by finish.py; cache metadata retains fit residuals and transforms. |
| preregister.py Z --watch | Populate registration caches as originals arrive. Stops when that zoom is complete; does not export tiles. |
| author_canopy.py | Freeze vegetation crowns from the complete registered zoom-3 painting as shared fictional world layers. Run once, then finish zooms 0 through 3 in order. |
| canonical.py | Save 8,192 px canonical water/road/building masks; repair classifications at inclusive outer grid samples and preserve surface roads over tunnels. Run after native references. |
| measure.py | Independently classify visible features from exported RGB; measure IoU, symmetric boundary distances, exact tile reconstruction, seam jumps, and parent-scale color differences. |
| grid_check.py | Quantify the difference between the engine's 2 m vertex samples and the finest native vector masks, independently of artwork. |
| review.py Z reference/raw/final [--row R] | Labeled contact sheets for review, under checks; never adds labels to game tiles. |
| audit.py | Assert tile count, RGB format, original-paint presence, base dimensions and bit depth; hash delivery artifacts. |

Build sources and references:

```sh
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/python tools/mapart/fetch.py
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/python tools/mapart/prepare.py
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/python tools/mapart/future.py
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/python tools/mapart/reference.py
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/python tools/mapart/canonical.py
```

Image generation is an explicit art-production step using the **built-in image tool**, not an API-key script. The overview prompt is under paintings/z0; later queues are made by contexts.py. Each queue entry lists its geometry reference, accepted parent, original style sheet and output filename. Inspect inputs, issue the prompt with those local references, then copy the returned original PNG to `paintings/zZ/C_R.raw.png`. Preserve supplementary prompt files. Do not resize or overwrite the raw originals. The tool returned 1,254 px squares during this run. The finishing code maps each to its 1,152 px overlap region (or 1,024 px overview).

After a complete zoom is painted:

```sh
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/python tools/mapart/finish.py 1
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/python tools/mapart/measure.py
tools/mapart/.venv/bin/python tools/mapart/contexts.py 2
```

Review the full map, representative full-resolution tiles, and joined boundaries. Exact geometry measurements do not establish artistic quality. Never accept solely on an RGB-mask score.

The offline viewer is `assets/source/maps/miami/checks/viewer.html`; open it directly in a browser. It reads the actual PNG tiles, supports pan/zoom and a fixed-camera painting comparison, and draws optional diagnostic overlays independently. No server or dependencies are required.

For final acceptance after every original exists, run `finish.py 3`, `author_canopy.py`, then `finish.py 0`, `finish.py 1`, `finish.py 2`, `finish.py 3`, `measure.py`, `grid_check.py` and `audit.py`. Preserve the frozen canopy during later finishing runs. `contexts.py` leaves prompts and reference crops for already-painted tiles intact. Exact fresh image generation is nondeterministic; the saved originals make subsequent finishing reproducible.

Do not change map.json after downloading and preparing an accepted map. To explore different bounds, use a separate destination and manifest: the download cache filenames describe this frozen square. See SOURCES.md and base/VALUES.md for source limits, licensing and authored-world conventions.

"""Register generated pigment, then constrain every visible feature to world geometry."""
import argparse,json,hashlib,inspect
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image,ImageDraw
from scipy import ndimage as nd
from common import *
from reference import grid_at
from alignment import feature_align,shore_align

def load(path,size=None):
    im=Image.open(path).convert('RGB')
    if size:im=im.resize(size,Image.Resampling.LANCZOS)
    return np.asarray(im,dtype=np.float32)

def water_rgb(a):return (a[...,1]-a[...,0]>3)&(a[...,2]-a[...,0]>-18)

def sample(a,y,x):
    if a.ndim==2:return nd.map_coordinates(a,[y,x],order=1,mode='nearest')
    return np.stack([nd.map_coordinates(a[...,i],[y,x],order=1,mode='nearest') for i in range(3)],-1)

def register(a,truth,reference=None):
    """Small smooth shoreline correction; final geometry is imposed separately."""
    aligned=False
    register.last_info={}
    if reference is not None:
        a,aligned,info=feature_align(a,reference)
        register.last_info['feature_fit']=info
        print('features',info,flush=True)
    if not aligned and .002<truth.mean()<.998:
        a,info=shore_align(a,truth)
        register.last_info['shore_similarity']=info
        print('shore similarity',info,flush=True)
        aligned=True
    if not aligned and a.shape[0]==1152:
        # Measured fallback for this image tool's expanded framing. Broad water
        # scenes lack unique corners; allow only small shoreline refinements.
        y,x=np.mgrid[:1152,:1152].astype(np.float32)
        a=sample(a,y/1.082,x/1.082)
    wet=water_rgb(a)
    ss=nd.gaussian_filter(nd.distance_transform_edt(wet)-nd.distance_transform_edt(~wet),1)
    ts=nd.gaussian_filter(nd.distance_transform_edt(truth)-nd.distance_transform_edt(~truth),1)
    sy,sx=np.gradient(ss)
    yy,xx=np.mgrid[:truth.shape[0],:truth.shape[1]].astype(np.float32)
    ux=np.zeros_like(xx);uy=np.zeros_like(yy)
    band=np.exp(-(np.abs(ts)/24)**4)
    for _ in range(12):
        delta=ts-sample(ss,yy+uy,xx+ux)
        gy=sample(sy,yy+uy,xx+ux);gx=sample(sx,yy+uy,xx+ux)
        den=gx*gx+gy*gy+(delta/2)**2+1e-4
        ux=nd.gaussian_filter(ux+nd.gaussian_filter(delta*gx/den,1)*band,.65)
        uy=nd.gaussian_filter(uy+nd.gaussian_filter(delta*gy/den,1)*band,.65)
        ux=np.clip(ux,-4,4);uy=np.clip(uy,-4,4)
    a=sample(a,yy+uy,xx+ux)
    # Repair only water, using open-water pigment clear of any inked land.
    # Keep land's original brushwork intact; semantic palettes handle invented
    # inland pools later without nearest-neighbor patchwork across tree crowns.
    wet=water_rgb(a)
    safe=nd.binary_erosion(wet,iterations=10,border_value=1)
    if safe.any():
        inds=nd.distance_transform_edt(~safe,return_distances=False,return_indices=True)
        bad=truth&~safe
        a[bad]=a[inds[0][bad],inds[1][bad]]
        smooth=nd.gaussian_filter(a,(1.6,1.6,0))
        blend=nd.gaussian_filter(bad.astype(np.float32),1.6)*truth
        a=a*(1-blend[...,None])+smooth*blend[...,None]
    return a

def cached_register(path,reference_path,truth,size):
    cache=path.with_name(path.name.replace('.raw.png','.registered.png'))
    meta=cache.with_suffix('.json')
    fingerprint=hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()+reference_path.read_bytes()+truth.tobytes()+
          inspect.getsource(register).encode()+inspect.getsource(feature_align).encode()+inspect.getsource(shore_align).encode()).hexdigest()
    if cache.exists() and meta.exists() and json.loads(meta.read_text()).get('fingerprint')==fingerprint:
        return load(cache)
    a=register(load(path,(size,size)),truth,load(reference_path))
    save(np.uint8(np.clip(a,0,255)),cache)
    meta.write_text(json.dumps({'fingerprint':fingerprint,'raw':path.name,**register.last_info},indent=2))
    return load(cache)

def assemble(z,partial=False):
    n=1024*2**z;count=2**z; ref=ROOT/'references'/f'z{z}'
    truth=np.array(Image.open(ref/'surface_water.png'))>0
    if z==0:return cached_register(ROOT/'paintings/z0/0_0.raw.png',ref/'whole.png',truth,n)
    # Overlapping native-scale paintings; smooth partition of unity in the gutters.
    out=np.zeros((n,n,3),np.float32);total=np.zeros((n,n),np.float32)
    g=64;size=1024+2*g
    ramp=np.ones(size,np.float32);ramp[:2*g]=np.sin(np.linspace(0,np.pi/2,2*g))**2
    ramp[-2*g:]=ramp[:2*g][::-1]
    weight=ramp[:,None]*ramp[None,:]
    padded=np.pad(truth,g,mode='edge')
    for y in range(count):
        for x in range(count):
            p=ROOT/'paintings'/f'z{z}'/f'{x}_{y}.raw.png'
            if not p.exists():
                if not partial:raise FileNotFoundError(p)
                continue
            target=padded[y*1024:y*1024+size,x*1024:x*1024+size]
            a=cached_register(p,ref/f'{x}_{y}.context.png',target,size)
            xa=max(0,x*1024-g);xb=min(n,(x+1)*1024+g)
            ya=max(0,y*1024-g);yb=min(n,(y+1)*1024+g)
            u=xa-(x*1024-g);v=ya-(y*1024-g)
            w=weight[v:v+yb-ya,u:u+xb-xa].copy()
            if x==0:w[:,:g]=ramp[v:v+yb-ya,None]
            if y==0:w[:g,:]=ramp[None,u:u+xb-xa]
            if x==count-1:w[:,-g:]=ramp[v:v+yb-ya,None]
            if y==count-1:w[-g:,:]=ramp[None,u:u+xb-xa]
            if x==0 and y==0:w[:g,:g]=1
            if x==count-1 and y==0:w[:g,-g:]=1
            if x==0 and y==count-1:w[-g:,:g]=1
            if x==count-1 and y==count-1:w[-g:,-g:]=1
            out[ya:yb,xa:xb]+=a[v:v+yb-ya,u:u+xb-xa]*w[...,None]
            total[ya:yb,xa:xb]+=w
    out/=np.maximum(total[...,None],1e-6)
    if partial:
        parent_path=ROOT/'paintings'/f'z{z-1}'/'final-master.png'
        if not parent_path.exists():parent_path=ROOT/'checks'/f'partial_z{z-1}.png'
        parent=load(parent_path,(n,n));missing=total<.999
        out[missing]=out[missing]*total[missing,None]+parent[missing]*(1-total[missing,None])
    return out

def pigment(lum,rg,gb):
    # Distinct physical pigment families make geometry measurable directly in RGB.
    g=np.clip(lum,gb+2,253-rg)
    return np.stack([g+rg,g,g-gb],-1)

def finish(z,partial=False):
    n=1024*2**z;mpp=SIZE/n; ref=ROOT/'references'/f'z{z}'
    raw=assemble(z,partial)
    save(np.uint8(np.clip(raw,0,255)),ROOT/'paintings'/f'z{z}'/'registered.png')
    w=np.array(Image.open(ref/'surface_water.png'))>0
    rd=np.array(Image.open(ref/'roads.png'))>0
    b=np.array(Image.open(ref/'buildings.png'))>0
    bio=np.array(Image.open(ref/'biome.png'))
    # Remove invented architectural boundaries, retain gently varying wash.
    l=raw.mean(2);soft=nd.gaussian_filter(l,2.2+z*.65)
    fine=np.clip(l-nd.gaussian_filter(l,.65),-22,22)
    # Bare paper receives a broad wash, not blurred ghosts of generated trees or
    # invented houses. Crisp detail is reserved for the constrained feature masks.
    paper=nd.gaussian_filter(l,18)
    out=pigment(190+(paper-174)*.22+fine*.16,19,40)
    nature=np.isin(bio,[3,4,5])
    if (ROOT/'base/painted_canopy_fine.png').exists():
        crown=np.asarray(Image.open(ROOT/'base/painted_canopy_fine.png').resize((n,n),Image.Resampling.NEAREST))>0
    else:
        # Pilot only. Final acceptance uses one frozen finest-scale canopy layer
        # for ALL zooms, including world data, rather than independent tree guesses.
        crown=((raw[...,1]-raw[...,0]>-5)&(raw[...,1]-raw[...,2]>30))|((raw[...,1]-raw[...,0]>-18)&(raw[...,1]-raw[...,2]>48)&(raw[...,1]<170))
        crown=nd.binary_closing(crown,iterations=1)
    nature=(nature|crown)&~(w|rd|b)
    green=raw.copy();green[...,1]=np.clip(150+(raw[...,1]-150)*.85,70,195)
    green[...,0]=green[...,1]+np.clip(raw[...,0]-raw[...,1],-8,12)
    green[...,2]=green[...,1]-np.clip(raw[...,1]-raw[...,2],46,66)
    out[nature]=green[nature]
    beach=bio==6
    out[beach]=pigment(211+(l-190)*.30,19,50)[beach]
    # Water is kept as generated watercolor, with exact coast repair.
    water=raw.copy()
    water[...,1]=np.maximum(water[...,1],water[...,0]+12)
    water[...,2]=np.maximum(water[...,2],water[...,0]+1)
    dw=nd.distance_transform_edt(w).astype(np.float32)
    # A continuous wet wash softens pigment extended across registration gaps.
    # Normalize inside water so nearby masonry never bleeds into the shallows.
    sigma=max(1.5,12/mpp)
    mf=w.astype(np.float32);den=nd.gaussian_filter(mf,sigma)
    blend=np.exp(-dw/max(2,48/mpp))*.85*w
    for k in range(3):
        wash=nd.gaussian_filter(water[...,k]*mf,sigma)/np.maximum(den,.001)
        water[...,k]=water[...,k]*(1-blend)+wash*blend
    out[w]=water[w]
    # Pale shallows and crisp ink at the measured water edge.
    # Hide nearest-pigment extension streaks with a continuous shallow wash.
    near=np.exp(-dw/max(2,32/mpp))*.72*w
    shallow=np.stack([153+fine*.15,181+fine*.15,165+fine*.15],-1)
    out=out*(1-near[...,None])+shallow*near[...,None]
    shore=w&(dw<=1)
    out[shore]=out[shore]*.40+np.array([45,72,63],np.float32)*.60
    landedge=(~w)&(nd.distance_transform_edt(~w)<=1)&~b&~rd
    out[landedge]*=.62
    # Exact road corridors, with economical shoulder lines, no invented lanes.
    rdist=nd.distance_transform_edt(rd).astype(np.float32)
    rl=211+np.clip((raw[...,1]-190)*.42,-28,18)+fine*.28
    if z>0:rl=rl-np.where(rdist<=1,22,0).astype(np.float32)
    out[rd]=pigment(rl,7,38)[rd]
    # Footprint-specific ruined masonry, preserving true courtyards and holes.
    db=nd.distance_transform_edt(b).astype(np.float32)
    bl=174+(soft-174)*.20+fine*.32 if z<2 else 174+(l-174)*.75+fine*.20
    if z==0:bl-=np.where(db<=1,43,0).astype(np.float32)
    else:bl-=np.where(db<=1,67,np.where(db<=2,10,0)).astype(np.float32)
    yy,xx=np.indices((n,n),dtype=np.int32)
    if z>=1:
        # Restrained quill hatch along interior walls; tied to map coordinates.
        hatch=((xx+yy*2)%(8+z)==0)&(db>1)&(db<4+z)
        bl[hatch]-=25
        # Unequal interior coursing; never spills beyond a building footprint.
        courses=((xx*3-yy)%19==0)&(db>3)
        bl[courses]-=10
    out[b]=pigment(bl,16,23)[b]
    # An explicit authored standing-water layer, not an extra invented coastline.
    flood=(grid_at('flooded_streets',n)>0)&rd&~b
    out[flood]=np.array([119,155,146])+fine[flood,None]*.2
    # Match broad pigment fields to accepted parent while retaining native detail.
    # Material-local luminance matching avoids smearing a coast into neighboring land.
    if z>0:
        parent_path=ROOT/'paintings'/f'z{z-1}'/'final-master.png'
        if not parent_path.exists():parent_path=ROOT/'checks'/f'partial_z{z-1}.png'
        parent=load(parent_path,(n,n))
        masks=[w,rd&~b&~flood,b,nature&~rd&~b,beach&~rd&~b,~(w|rd|b|nature|beach)]
        for mask in masks:
            mf=mask.astype(np.float32)
            den=nd.gaussian_filter(mf,12)
            a=nd.gaussian_filter(out[...,1]*mf,12)/np.maximum(den,.01)
            p=nd.gaussian_filter(parent[...,1]*mf,12)/np.maximum(den,.01)
            delta=np.clip(p-a,-50,50)*.96
            out[mask]+=delta[mask,None]
        # Water hue, not just brightness, must agree with the accepted parent.
        mf=w.astype(np.float32);den=nd.gaussian_filter(mf,8)
        for k in [0,2]:
            a=nd.gaussian_filter(out[...,k]*mf,8)/np.maximum(den,.01)
            p=nd.gaussian_filter(parent[...,k]*mf,8)/np.maximum(den,.01)
            delta=np.clip(p-a,-55,55)
            out[...,k][w]+=delta[w]
    # Reassert visible pigment categories after color transfer and clipping.
    out=np.clip(out,0,255)
    dry=~(w|rd|b|flood)
    # Keep shaded shore ink in its own material family too. Otherwise darkened
    # olive can accidentally acquire the ochre road family's RGB differences.
    out[dry&~nature&~beach]=pigment(out[...,1],19,40)[dry&~nature&~beach]
    out[dry&beach]=pigment(out[...,1],19,50)[dry&beach]
    forest=dry&nature&~beach
    g=np.clip(out[...,1],68,241)
    green=np.stack([g+np.clip(out[...,0]-out[...,1],-8,12),g,
                    g-np.clip(out[...,1]-out[...,2],46,66)],-1)
    out[forest]=green[forest]
    for mask,rg,gb in [(b,16,23),(rd&~b&~flood,7,38)]:out[mask]=pigment(out[...,1],rg,gb)[mask]
    out[...,0][w|flood]=np.minimum(out[...,0][w|flood],245)
    out[...,1][w|flood]=np.maximum(out[...,1][w|flood],out[...,0][w|flood]+10)
    out[...,2][w|flood]=np.maximum(out[...,2][w|flood],out[...,0][w|flood]+1)
    out=np.uint8(np.clip(out,0,255))
    if (ROOT/'base/future_changes.geojson').exists():
        # Sunken wrecks are authored world objects. Teal ink keeps them visibly
        # beneath the water, and their exact polygons are saved for the engine.
        from shapely.geometry import LineString
        im=Image.fromarray(out);draw=ImageDraw.Draw(im)
        def pixel(x,y):return ((x-B[0])/mpp,(B[3]-y)/mpp)
        for geom,props in vectors('future_changes'):
            if props['kind']!='submerged_wreck' or z==0:continue
            pts=[pixel(x,y) for x,y in geom.exterior.coords]
            draw.line(pts,fill=(61,88,77),width=1)
            import math
            angle=math.radians(props['angle_degrees']);dx=math.cos(angle);dy=math.sin(angle)
            cx,cy=props['center'];length=props['length_m'];width=props['width_m']
            if z>=2:
                for u in np.arange(-length*.4,length*.35,5):
                    draw.line([pixel(cx+u*dx-v*dy,cy+u*dy+v*dx) for v in [-width*.4,width*.4]],fill=(72,100,87),width=1)
        out=np.asarray(im)
    dest=ROOT/'tiles'/f'z{z}'
    save(out,ROOT/'checks'/f'partial_z{z}.png' if partial else ROOT/'paintings'/f'z{z}'/'final-master.png')
    im=Image.fromarray(out)
    for y in range(2**z):
        for x in range(2**z):
            if partial and not (ROOT/'paintings'/f'z{z}'/f'{x}_{y}.raw.png').exists():continue
            dest.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
            im.crop((x*1024,y*1024,(x+1)*1024,(y+1)*1024)).save(dest/f'{x}_{y}.png')
    im.resize((1024,1024),Image.Resampling.LANCZOS).save(ROOT/'checks'/f'overview_z{z}.png')
    print('finished',z,flush=True)

"""Render native-scale geographic references independently, never enlarge a mask."""
import argparse,json
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
from scipy import ndimage as nd
from rasterio.warp import reproject,Resampling
from common import *

PALETTE=np.array([[0,0,0],[86,133,128],[211,207,173],[156,165,119],
                 [123,134,96],[155,163,133],[231,212,162],[177,164,138],
                 [220,208,170],[220,208,170]],dtype=np.uint8)

def grid_at(name,n):
    a=np.array(Image.open(ROOT/'base'/f'{name}.png'))
    out=np.zeros((n,n),dtype=a.dtype)
    reproject(a,out,src_transform=GRID,src_crs=CRS,dst_transform=transform(n),
              dst_crs=CRS,resampling=Resampling.nearest)
    return out

def build(z):
    n=1024*2**z; ref=ROOT/'references'/f'z{z}';ref.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
    water=vectors('areawater');roads=vectors('roads');buildings=vectors('buildings')
    w=burn([(g,1) for g,p in water],n)>0
    rd=burn([(g.buffer(p['width_m']/2,cap_style=2,join_style=2),
               2 if p['mtfcc'] in ['S1100','S1200'] else 1) for g,p in sorted(roads,key=lambda gp:gp[1]['width_m'])
               if 'tunl' not in (p['name'] or '').lower()],n)
    if (ROOT/'base/future_changes.geojson').exists():
        gaps=[(g,1) for g,p in vectors('future_changes') if p['kind']=='missing_bridge_span']
        rd[burn(gaps,n)>0]=0
    b=burn([(g,1) for g,p in buildings],n)>0
    bio=grid_at('biome',n);bio[(bio==7)|(bio==8)|(bio==9)]=2
    bio[w]=1;bio[rd>0]=8;bio[b]=7
    surface=w&(rd==0)&~b
    for name,a in [('water',w),('surface_water',surface),('roads',rd),('buildings',b),('biome',bio)]:
        save(a.astype('uint8'),ref/f'{name}.png')
    a=PALETTE[bio].copy()
    # Broad pale shallows belong on water, and have a fixed world width.
    d=nd.distance_transform_edt(w)
    shallow=(d<60/(SIZE/n))&surface
    a[shallow]=[163,198,181]
    edge=surface&~nd.binary_erosion(surface,border_value=1)
    a[edge]=[63,91,76]
    bedge=b&~nd.binary_erosion(b,border_value=1)
    a[bedge]=[92,82,61]
    # Subpixel roads still visible in the far-scale reference via their exact lines.
    centers=burn([(g,1) for g,p in roads if 'tunl' not in (p['name'] or '').lower()],n)>0
    if (ROOT/'base/future_changes.geojson').exists():centers[burn(gaps,n)>0]=False
    a[centers&~b]=[222,208,171]

    im=Image.fromarray(a)
    for y in range(2**z):
        for x in range(2**z):
            im.crop((x*1024,y*1024,(x+1)*1024,(y+1)*1024)).save(ref/f'{x}_{y}.png')
    print('reference',z,n,flush=True)

"""Independent RGB classification and geometry/seam/zoom acceptance measurements."""
import json,sys
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
from scipy import ndimage as nd
from common import ROOT
from reference import grid_at

def boundary(m):
    s=m&~nd.binary_erosion(m,border_value=1)
    s[[0,-1],:]=False;s[:,[0,-1]]=False
    return s

def score(m,t):
    a=boundary(m);b=boundary(t)
    if a.any() and b.any():
        d1=nd.distance_transform_edt(~b)[a];d2=nd.distance_transform_edt(~a)[b]
        d=np.r_[d1,d2]
        distances={'mean_boundary_px':float(d.mean()),'p95_boundary_px':float(np.percentile(d,95)),'max_boundary_px':float(d.max())}
    else:distances={'mean_boundary_px':None,'p95_boundary_px':None,'max_boundary_px':None}
    return {'iou':float((m&t).sum()/max(1,(m|t).sum())),
            'false_positive_pixels':int((m&~t).sum()),'false_negative_pixels':int((t&~m).sum()),**distances}

def main():
    results={}
    for z in range(4):
        dest=ROOT/'tiles'/f'z{z}';p=ROOT/'paintings'/f'z{z}'/'final-master.png'
        if not p.exists():continue
        a=np.asarray(Image.open(p),dtype=np.int16);n=a.shape[0]
        rg=a[...,0]-a[...,1];gb=a[...,1]-a[...,2]
        detected={'surface_water':(rg<-3)&((a[...,2]-a[...,0])>-18),
                  'buildings':(rg>=14)&(rg<=22)&(gb>=18)&(gb<=30),
                  'roads':(rg>=4)&(rg<=10)&(gb>=32)&(gb<=44)}
        ref=ROOT/'references'/f'z{z}'
        b=np.array(Image.open(ref/'buildings.png'))>0
        rd=np.array(Image.open(ref/'roads.png'))>0
        w=np.array(Image.open(ref/'surface_water.png'))>0
        f=(grid_at('flooded_streets',n)>0)&rd&~b
        truth={'surface_water':w|f,'buildings':b,'roads':rd&~b&~f}
        geo={key:score(detected[key],truth[key]) for key in truth}
        # Exact equality after reconstructing PNGs detects missing rows, columns,
        # transposed tiles or cut-coordinate errors independently of master layout.
        stitch=np.empty_like(a,dtype=np.uint8)
        for y in range(2**z):
            for x in range(2**z):
                tile=np.asarray(Image.open(dest/f'{x}_{y}.png'))
                assert tile.shape==(1024,1024,3)
                stitch[y*1024:(y+1)*1024,x*1024:(x+1)*1024]=tile
        seams=[]
        for k in range(1,2**z):
            c=k*1024
            for axis in ['vertical','horizontal']:
                v=a if axis=='vertical' else a.transpose(1,0,2)
                jump=np.abs(v[:,c]-v[:,c-1]).mean()
                # Baseline uses nearby boundaries on both sides, including edges
                # of real geography. It is diagnostic, not a visual-quality proof.
                qs=[q for q in range(c-32,c+33) if q!=c]
                near=np.mean([np.abs(v[:,q]-v[:,q-1]).mean() for q in qs])
                seams.append({'axis':axis,'coordinate':c,'mean_channel_jump':float(jump),
                              'nearby_mean':float(near),'ratio':float(jump/max(near,.001))})
        result={'shape':list(a.shape),'tile_count':(2**z)**2,'geometry':geo,
                'stitch_max_channel_error':int(np.abs(stitch.astype(np.int16)-a).max()),'seams':seams}
        if z>0:
            small=np.asarray(Image.fromarray(stitch).resize((n//2,n//2),Image.Resampling.BOX),dtype=np.float32)
            parent=np.asarray(Image.open(ROOT/'paintings'/f'z{z-1}'/'final-master.png'),dtype=np.float32)
            err=np.abs(small-parent)
            result['parent_agreement']={'mean_abs_rgb_255':float(err.mean()),'p95_abs_channel':float(np.percentile(err,95)),
                'rmse_rgb_255':float(np.sqrt(np.mean((small-parent)**2))),
                'mean_color_shift_rgb':list(map(float,(small-parent).mean((0,1)))),
                'blurred_8px_mae':float(np.abs(nd.gaussian_filter(small,(8,8,0))-nd.gaussian_filter(parent,(8,8,0))).mean())}
        results[f'z{z}']=result
        print(z,geo,result.get('parent_agreement'),flush=True)
    (ROOT/'checks/measurements.json').write_text(json.dumps(results,indent=2))

if __name__=='__main__':main()
// Map files (shared/world/mapfile.ts), made outside the engine: from a folder of layers, and back into one.
//
//   bun tools/map.ts build <folder> <out.snmap>     a map from a folder of layers
//   bun tools/map.ts unpack <file.snmap> <folder>   the folder a map is built from
//   bun tools/map.ts proving <out.snmap>            the proving ground, as the server runs it with no --map
//   bun tools/map.ts info <file.snmap>              what a file holds
//
// A folder of layers. A chunk is 64 m and the ground has a sample every 2 m, so a map of 8 chunks a side is 257 samples
// a side. Pictures are north up, as the map screen shows them: the first pixel is the north-west corner, which is the
// highest x and the highest z. Places in the JSON files are metres from the map's south-east corner, x growing west and
// z growing north. A yaw is degrees from north, turning toward +x.
//
//   map.json      { "id": "core:miami", "chunks": [125, 125], "minY": -32, "stepY": 0.00390625, "seaLevel": 0 }
//                 The id is the map's name to the server, and that of its definition in the content, if it has one.
//                 A height is minY + value * stepY metres. Without seaLevel the map has no water.
//   heights.png   16-bit greyscale, a pixel a sample. Or heights.u16: the same values, little-endian, with no header.
//   tint.png      8-bit greyscale or indexed, a pixel a sample: its palette index (shared/pack/palette.ts).
//                 Or tint.u8. Without either, index 0 everywhere.
//   statics.json  [{ "kind": "core:wall", "x": 240.5, "y": 1.8, "z": 270, "yaw": 90 }]
//                 Pieces set down with the world, by content id and centre. Optional.
//   nodes.json    Layers of resource nodes, which share a chunk's 256 slots. Optional. A layer is one of:
//                 { "seed": 7, "perChunk": 96, "kinds": { "core:tree": 5, "core:rock": 3 }, "allow": "woods.png" }
//                   scatters `perChunk` slots over every chunk, each a kind drawn by weight. A slot stays empty under
//                   water, on a steep slope, and where `allow` is darker than half: an 8-bit greyscale picture of
//                   1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 m a pixel. Without `allow`, anywhere.
//                 { "list": [{ "kind": "core:rock", "x": 12.5, "z": 40, "yaw": 0 }] }
//                   stands each node on the ground where it says.
//   spawns.json   [{ "name": "Plaza", "x": 256, "z": 240, "yaw": 0 }]
//                 Up to 16. The first is where a new survivor arrives, and a dead one chooses among them.

import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { CORE_CONTENT } from "../content/core.ts";
import { provingFile } from "../server/world.ts";
import { compileContent } from "../shared/content/registry.ts";
import { CHUNK_SIZE } from "../shared/coords.ts";
import { parseMap, writeMap, type MapData } from "../shared/world/mapfile.ts";
import { readLayers, writeLayers } from "./map/layers.ts";

const registry = () => compileContent(CORE_CONTENT).registry!;

/** What a map holds, in lines, and the content ids it names that the core pack lacks. */
export function describe(file: Uint8Array): string[] {
  const map = parseMap(file);
  const { chunksX, chunksZ } = map.dims;
  let low = 65535;
  let high = 0;
  for (const h of map.heights) {
    if (h < low) low = h;
    if (h > high) high = h;
  }
  const at = (h: number): string => (map.minY + h * map.stepY).toFixed(1);
  const lines = [
    `${map.id}, hash ${map.hash.toString(16).padStart(8, "0")}, ${file.length} bytes (${Bun.gzipSync(file as Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>).length} compressed)`,
    `${chunksX} by ${chunksZ} chunks, ${chunksX * CHUNK_SIZE} by ${chunksZ * CHUNK_SIZE} m, ground from ${at(low)} to ${at(high)} m, ${map.seaLevel === -Infinity ? "no water" : `sea at ${map.seaLevel} m`}`,
    `${map.statics.length} static pieces`,
    ...map.nodes.map((layer) => ("first" in layer ? `${layer.kind.length} listed nodes` : `${layer.perChunk} node slots a chunk, scattered${layer.allow ? ` where a picture of ${layer.allowCell} m a pixel allows` : ""}: ${layer.kinds.map(([id, weight]) => `${id} x${weight}`).join(", ")}`)),
    `spawn points: ${map.spawns.map((s) => `${s.name} (${s.x}, ${s.z})`).join(", ")}`,
  ];
  const known = registry().index;
  const named = new Set([...map.statics.map((s) => s.kind), ...map.nodes.flatMap((layer) => ("first" in layer ? layer.kinds : layer.kinds.map(([id]) => id)))]);
  const lacking = [...named].filter((id) => !known.has(id));
  if (lacking.length > 0) lines.push(`not in the core content: ${lacking.join(", ")}`);
  return lines;
}

function save(path: string, map: MapData | Uint8Array): void {
  const file = map instanceof Uint8Array ? map : writeMap(map);
  writeFileSync(path, file);
  for (const line of describe(file)) console.log(line);
}

/** `args` are the words after the command's name. Another tool adds its command here. */
export const COMMANDS: Record<string, { usage: string; run(args: string[]): void }> = {
  build: { usage: "<folder> <out.snmap>", run: ([folder, out]) => save(out!, readLayers(folder!)) },
  unpack: { usage: "<file.snmap> <folder>", run: ([file, folder]) => writeLayers(parseMap(new Uint8Array(readFileSync(file!))), folder!) },
  proving: { usage: "<out.snmap>", run: ([out]) => save(out!, provingFile(registry())) },
  info: { usage: "<file.snmap>", run: ([file]) => describe(new Uint8Array(readFileSync(file!))).forEach((line) => console.log(line)) },
};

if (import.meta.main) {
  const [name, ...args] = process.argv.slice(2);
  const command = COMMANDS[name ?? ""];
  if (!command || args.length !== command.usage.split(" ").length) {
    console.error(Object.entries(COMMANDS).map(([n, c]) => `bun tools/map.ts ${n} ${c.usage}`).join("\n"));
    process.exit(2);
  }
  try {
    command.run(args);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err));
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

# Image Generation Skill

Generates or edits images for the current project (for example website assets, game assets, UI mockups, product mockups, wireframes, logo design, photorealistic images, or infographics).

## Top-level modes and rules

This skill has exactly two top-level modes:

- **Default built-in tool mode (preferred):** built-in `image_gen` tool for image generation, editing, and transparent-image requests. Does not require `OPENAI_API_KEY`.
- **Fallback CLI mode:** `scripts/image_gen.py` CLI. Use when the user explicitly asks for or confirms the CLI/API/model path. Requires `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

Within CLI fallback, the CLI exposes three subcommands:

- `generate`
- `edit`
- `generate-batch`

Rules:
- Use the built-in `image_gen` tool by default for normal image generation and editing requests.
- Do not switch to CLI fallback for ordinary quality, size, or file-path control.
- For transparent images, ask built-in `image_gen` for a transparent background and preserve the generated alpha.
- Never silently switch from built-in `image_gen` or CLI `gpt-image-2` to CLI `gpt-image-1.5`; ask the user first unless they explicitly requested `gpt-image-1.5`.
- The word `batch` by itself does not mean CLI fallback. If the user asks for many assets or says to batch-generate assets without explicitly asking for CLI/API/model controls, stay on the built-in path and issue one built-in call per requested asset or variant.
- If the built-in tool fails or is unavailable, tell the user the CLI fallback exists and that it requires `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Proceed only if the user explicitly asks for that fallback.
- If the user explicitly asks for CLI mode, use the bundled `scripts/image_gen.py` workflow. Do not create one-off SDK runners.
- Never modify `scripts/image_gen.py`. If something is missing, ask the user before doing anything else.

Built-in save-path policy:
- In built-in tool mode, Codex saves generated images under `$CODEX_HOME/*` by default.
- Do not describe or rely on OS temp as the default built-in destination.
- Do not describe or rely on a destination-path argument (if any) on the built-in `image_gen` tool. If a specific location is needed, generate first and then move or copy the selected output from `$CODEX_HOME/generated_images/...`.
- Save-path precedence in built-in mode:
  1. If the user names a destination, move or copy the selected output there.
  2. If the image is meant for the current project, move or copy the final selected image into the workspace before finishing.
  3. If the image is only for preview or brainstorming, render it inline; the underlying file can remain at the default `$CODEX_HOME/*` path.
- Never leave a project-referenced asset only at the default `$CODEX_HOME/*` path.
- Do not overwrite an existing asset unless the user explicitly asked for replacement; otherwise create a sibling versioned filename such as `hero-v2.png` or `item-icon-edited.png`.

Shared prompt guidance for both modes lives in `references/prompting.md` and `references/sample-prompts.md`.

Fallback-only docs/resources for CLI mode:
- `references/cli.md`
- `references/image-api.md`
- `references/codex-network.md`
- `scripts/image_gen.py`

## When to use
- Generate a new image (concept art, product shot, cover, website hero)
- Generate a new image using one or more reference images for style, composition, or mood
- Edit an existing image (inpainting, lighting or weather transformations, background replacement, object removal, compositing, transparent background)
- Produce many assets or variants for one task

## When not to use
- Extending or matching an existing SVG/vector icon set, logo system, or illustration library inside the repo
- Creating simple shapes, diagrams, wireframes, or icons that are better produced directly in SVG, HTML/CSS, or canvas
- Making a small project-local asset edit when the source file already exists in an editable native format
- Any task where the user clearly wants deterministic code-native output instead of a generated bitmap

## Decision tree

Think about two separate questions:

1. **Intent:** is this a new image or an edit of an existing image?
2. **Execution strategy:** is this one asset or many assets/variants?

Intent:
- If the user wants to modify an existing image while preserving parts of it, treat the request as **edit**.
- If the user provides images only as references for style, composition, mood, or subject guidance, treat the request as **generate**.
- If the user provides no images, treat the request as **generate**.

Built-in edit semantics:
- Built-in edit mode is for images already visible in the conversation context, such as attached images or images generated earlier in the thread.
- If the user wants to edit a local image file with the built-in tool, first load it with built-in `view_image` tool so the image is visible in the conversation context, then proceed with the built-in edit flow.
- Do not promise arbitrary filesystem-path editing through the built-in tool.
- If a local file still needs direct file-path control, masks, or other explicit CLI-only parameters, use the explicit CLI fallback only when the user asks for it.
- For edits, preserve invariants aggressively and save non-destructively by default.

Execution strategy:
- In the built-in default path, produce many assets or variants by issuing one `image_gen` call per requested asset or variant.
- In the CLI fallback path, use the CLI `generate-batch` subcommand only when the user explicitly chose CLI mode and needs many prompts/assets.
- For many distinct assets, do not use `n` as a substitute for separate prompts. `n` is for variants of one prompt; distinct assets need distinct built-in calls or distinct CLI `generate-batch` jobs.

Assume the user wants a new image unless they clearly ask to change an existing one.

## Workflow
1. Decide the top-level mode: built-in by default, including transparent-output requests; fallback CLI only if explicitly requested or confirmed.
2. Decide the intent: `generate` or `edit`.
3. Decide whether the output is preview-only or meant to be consumed by the current project.
4. Decide the execution strategy: single asset vs repeated built-in calls vs CLI `generate-batch`.
5. Collect inputs up front: prompt(s), exact text (verbatim), constraints/avoid list, and any input images.
6. For every input image, label its role explicitly:
   - reference image
   - edit target
   - supporting insert/style/compositing input
7. If the edit target is only on the local filesystem and you are staying on the built-in path, inspect it with `view_image` first so the image is available in conversation context.
8. If the user asked for a photo, illustration, sprite, product image, banner, or other explicitly raster-style asset, use `image_gen` rather than substituting SVG/HTML/CSS placeholders. If the request is for an icon, logo, or UI graphic that should match existing repo-native SVG/vector/code assets, prefer editing those directly instead.
9. Augment the prompt based on specificity:
   - If the user's prompt is already specific and detailed, normalize it into a clear spec without adding creative requirements.
   - If the user's prompt is generic, add tasteful augmentation only when it materially improves output quality.
10. Use the built-in `image_gen` tool by default.
11. For transparent-output requests, ask built-in `image_gen` for a transparent background and preserve the generated alpha channel.
12. Inspect outputs and validate: subject, style, composition, text accuracy, and invariants/avoid items.
13. Iterate with a single targeted change, then re-check.
14. For preview-only work, render the image inline; the underlying file may remain at the default `$CODEX_HOME/generated_images/...` path.
15. For project-bound work, move or copy the selected artifact into the workspace and update any consuming code or references. Never leave a project-referenced asset only at the default `$CODEX_HOME/generated_images/...` path.
16. For batches or multi-asset requests, persist every requested deliverable final in the workspace unless the user explicitly asked to keep outputs preview-only. Discarded variants do not need to be kept unless requested.
17. If the user explicitly chooses or confirms the CLI fallback, then use the fallback-only docs for model, quality, size, `input_fidelity`, masks, output format, output paths, and network setup.
18. Always report the final saved path(s) for any workspace-bound asset(s), plus the final prompt or prompt set and whether the built-in tool or fallback CLI mode was used.

## Transparent image requests

Ask built-in `image_gen` for a genuinely transparent background and preserve its alpha.

## Prompt augmentation

Reformat user prompts into a structured, production-oriented spec. Make the user's goal clearer and more actionable, but do not blindly add detail.

Treat this as prompt-shaping guidance, not a closed schema. Use only the lines that help, and add a short extra labeled line when it materially improves clarity.

### Specificity policy

Use the user's prompt specificity to decide how much augmentation is appropriate:

- If the prompt is already specific and detailed, preserve that specificity and only normalize/structure it.
- If the prompt is generic, you may add tasteful augmentation when it will materially improve the result.

Allowed augmentations:
- composition or framing hints
- polish level or intended-use hints
- practical layout guidance
- reasonable scene concreteness that supports the stated request

Not allowed augmentations:
- extra characters or objects that are not implied by the request
- brand names, slogans, palettes, or narrative beats that are not implied
- arbitrary side-specific placement unless the surrounding layout supports it

## Use-case taxonomy (exact slugs)

Classify each request into one of these buckets and keep the slug consistent across prompts and references.

Generate:
- photorealistic-natural — candid/editorial lifestyle scenes with real texture and natural lighting.
- product-mockup — product/packaging shots, catalog imagery, merch concepts.
- ui-mockup — app/web interface mockups and wireframes; specify the desired fidelity.
- infographic-diagram — diagrams/infographics with structured layout and text.
- scientific-educational — classroom explainers, scientific diagrams, and learning visuals with required labels and accuracy constraints.
- ads-marketing — campaign concepts and ad creatives with audience, brand position, scene, and exact tagline/copy.
- productivity-visual — slide, chart, workflow, and data-heavy business visuals.
- logo-brand — logo/mark exploration, vector-friendly.
- illustration-story — comics, children’s book art, narrative scenes.
- stylized-concept — style-driven concept art, 3D/stylized renders.
- historical-scene — period-accurate/world-knowledge scenes.

Edit:
- text-localization — translate/replace in-image text, preserve layout.
- identity-preserve — try-on, person-in-scene; lock face/body/pose.
- precise-object-edit — remove/replace a specific element (including interior swaps).
- lighting-weather — time-of-day/season/atmosphere changes only.
- background-extraction — transparent background / clean cutout. Ask built-in `image_gen` for actual transparency.
- style-transfer — apply reference style while changing subject/scene.
- compositing — multi-image insert/merge with matched lighting/perspective.
- sketch-to-render — drawing/line art to photoreal render.

## Shared prompt schema

Use the following labeled spec as shared prompt scaffolding for both top-level modes:

```text
Use case: <taxonomy slug>
Asset type: <where the asset will be used>
Primary request: <user's main prompt>
Input images: <Image 1: role; Image 2: role> (optional)
Scene/backdrop: <environment>
Subject: <main subject>
Style/medium: <photo/illustration/3D/etc>
Composition/framing: <wide/close/top-down; placement>
Lighting/mood: <lighting + mood>
Color palette: <palette notes>
Materials/textures: <surface details>
Text (verbatim): "<exact text>"
Constraints: <must keep/must avoid>
Avoid: <negative constraints>
```

Notes:
- `Asset type` and `Input images` are prompt scaffolding, not dedicated CLI flags.
- `Scene/backdrop` refers to the visual setting. It is not the same as the fallback CLI `background` parameter, which controls output transparency behavior.
- Fallback-only execution notes such as `Quality:`, `Input fidelity:`, masks, output format, and output paths belong in the CLI path only. Do not treat them as built-in `image_gen` tool arguments.

Augmentation rules:
- Keep it short.
- Add only the details needed to improve the prompt materially.
- For edits, explicitly list invariants (`change only X; keep Y unchanged`).
- If any critical detail is missing and blocks success, ask a question; otherwise proceed.

```text
Use case: product-mockup
```


## Prompting best practices
- Structure prompt as scene/backdrop -> subject -> details -> constraints.
- Include intended use (ad, UI mock, infographic) to set the mode and polish level.
- Use camera/composition language for photorealism.
- Only use SVG/vector stand-ins when the user explicitly asked for vector output or a non-image placeholder.
- Quote exact text and specify typography + placement.
- For tricky words, spell them letter-by-letter and require verbatim rendering.
- For multi-image inputs, reference images by index and describe how they should be used.
- For edits, repeat invariants every iteration to reduce drift.
- Iterate with single-change follow-ups.
- If the prompt is generic, add only the extra detail that will materially help.
- If the prompt is already detailed, normalize it instead of expanding it.
- For CLI fallback only, see `references/cli.md` and `references/image-api.md` for model, `quality`, `input_fidelity`, masks, output format, and output-path guidance.
- For transparent images, ask built-in `image_gen` for actual transparency and preserve its alpha.

More principles shared by both modes: `references/prompting.md`.
Copy/paste specs shared by both modes: `references/sample-prompts.md`.

Asset-type templates (website assets, game assets, wireframes, logo) are consolidated in `references/sample-prompts.md`.

## gpt-image-2 guidance for CLI fallback

The fallback CLI defaults to `gpt-image-2`.

- Use `gpt-image-2` for new CLI/API workflows unless the user confirms a different model.
- CLI `gpt-image-2` does not support `background=transparent`; ask before using `gpt-image-1.5` unless the user explicitly requested that model.
- `gpt-image-2` always uses high fidelity for image inputs; do not set `input_fidelity` with this model.
- `gpt-image-2` supports `quality` values `low`, `medium`, `high`, and `auto`.
- Use `quality low` for fast drafts, thumbnails, and quick iterations. Use `medium`, `high`, or `auto` for final assets, dense text, diagrams, identity-sensitive edits, or high-resolution outputs.
- Square images are typically fastest to generate. Use `1024x1024` for fast square drafts.
- If the user asks for 4K-style output, use `3840x2160` for landscape or `2160x3840` for portrait.
- `gpt-image-2` size may be `auto` or `WIDTHxHEIGHT` if all constraints hold: max edge `<= 3840px`, both edges multiples of `16px`, long-to-short ratio `<= 3:1`, total pixels between `655,360` and `8,294,400`.

Popular `gpt-image-2` sizes:
- `1024x1024` square
- `1536x1024` landscape
- `1024x1536` portrait
- `2048x2048` 2K square
- `2048x1152` 2K landscape
- `3840x2160` 4K landscape
- `2160x3840` 4K portrait
- `auto`

# Shared world layers

Base PNGs without the `_fine` suffix are 4,065 × 4,065 **vertex samples**, with north at row 0. The inclusive endpoints span exactly 8,128 m: sample `(column,row)` is `(−4064 + 2×column, 4064 − 2×row)` metres in the local Transverse Mercator CRS in `../map.json`. There are 4,064 two-metre cells, 127 chunks of 64 m. Read grayscale values as numbers, with no color management or gamma conversion. The PNGs contain no georeferencing tags; `map.json` and this file are authoritative.

The game tile images instead use pixel areas: at zoom z, pixel centers are `(−4064 +(column+.5)×8128/(1024×2^z), 4064−(row+.5)×8128/(1024×2^z))`. This distinction prevents a half-pixel drift.

For the game's 0–100 map overlay, use eastward coordinate `100×(x+4064)/8128` and southward coordinate `100×(4064−y)/8128`. These are normalized game coordinates, not geographic longitude/latitude in degrees. Overlay rendering belongs to the game; it is absent from every tile.

| File | Encoding |
|---|---|
| height.png | Unsigned 16-bit. Height in metres NAVD88 = value/100 − 100. NOAA heights converted from US survey feet with 1200/3937. Bilinear reprojection; 1 cm quantization. |
| height_valid.png | 8-bit: 255 surveyed DEM coverage; 0 absent. Missing heights use −1 m in height.png. **This is an explicit engine convention, not measured bathymetry.** |
| water.png | 8-bit: 1 TIGER water polygon; 0 land. Water beneath elevated bridges is retained. |
| roads.png | 8-bit: 0 none; 1 local/service/path; 2 arterial/highway; 3 road over source water; 4 subterranean tunnel (not painted as a surface bridge); 5 authored missing bridge span. TIGER centerlines are measured geometry; corridor widths are authored: 22 m highway, 14 m arterial, 8 m local, 3–7 m paths/ramps/service. |
| buildings.png | 8-bit: 1 footprint; 0 outside. FEMA/ORNL USA Structures. Includes actual courtyards/holes where supplied. |
| landcover.png | 8-bit NLCD 2021 codes, nearest sampling. 11 water; 21 developed open; 22 low-intensity development; 23 medium; 24 high; 31 barren; 41 deciduous forest; 42 evergreen; 43 mixed; 52 shrub; 71 grass; 81 pasture; 82 crops; 90 woody wetland; 95 emergent wetland; 255 source nodata. Native source is ~30 m, not 2 m. |
| biome.png | Authored succession: 1 water; 2 open urban land; 3 reclaimed vegetation; 4 coastal mangrove; 5 low wetland; 6 sand; 7 ruin footprint; 8 road; 9 bridge. Derived from NLCD, DEM, shore distance and exact geometry. These are fictional future conditions, not surveyed present vegetation. |
| flooded_streets.png | Authored standing water: 1 low street pool; 0 other. Road land below 0.55 m NAVD88, within 300 m of the surveyed coast, excluding buildings; small artifacts removed. Coast geometry is unchanged. |
| bridge_gaps.png | Authored missing spans: 1 gap region; 0 other. Intersect with road-over-water to remove the deck. Four precise vector polygons are in future_changes.geojson. |
| wrecks.png | Authored submerged hulls: 1 footprint; 0 other. Four original fictional objects, not recorded real wreck sites. Positions and outlines in future_changes.geojson; the water above them remains water. |
| painted_canopy.png | 8-bit: 1 added future-world vegetation crown; 0 other. Authored from the registered finest-scale original paintings, excluding water, roads, buildings and beach. Union with biome vegetation classes 3–5 for world placement. Not a tree survey and does not encode heights. |

Four files use a finer grid: `water_fine.png`, `buildings_fine.png`, `roads_fine.png`, and `painted_canopy_fine.png` are 8,192 × 8,192 pixel areas across the same bounds. They use the same respective class encodings. **Use these canonical fine masks or the vectors for world feature placement:** very thin source features can disappear between 2 m samples. The fine geographic masks match the finest painting geometry exactly. The 4,065-sample layers are convenient engine-grid companions, not a lossless substitute for the fine outlines.

The fine canopy preserves close-scale crown outlines; every painted zoom samples this same frozen layer. `painted_canopy.json` records provenance and counts. At the inclusive grid's four outer sample lines, classifications use the adjacent finest pixel inside the square, avoiding a false empty fringe caused by half-open polygon rasterization. `checks/canonical_layers.json` records endpoint corrections. Road tunnels occupy class 4 only where there is no visible surface road; an intersecting surface road retains its surface class.

`areawater.geojson`, `roads.geojson` and `buildings.geojson` retain clipped vector geometry in the **local projected CRS**, not RFC 7946 geographic degrees. Their `crs` member declares it. Use them to render reference images afresh at every zoom. Do not enlarge the 2 m masks for close-scale shoreline tracing.

Known source limits: TIGER is cartographic rather than a modern cadastral coastline survey; FEMA excludes many structures below 450 square feet and does not certify sub-metre positional accuracy. A 1 px painting-registration score measures agreement with these inputs, not their accuracy on Earth. Source dates differ. No ocean bathymetry has been acquired.
